Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Northern common cuscus (Phalanger orientalis) were obtained through indirect calorimetry on resting adults under thermoneutral conditions. At a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption reached 883.4 milliliters per hour [JOi = 883.4 milliliters per hour], a value consistent with the relatively low metabolic demands typical of arboreal folivores in the family Phalangeridae. The thermal regime during these measurements was carefully regulated to match the species' active phase body temperature, ensuring that the recorded oxygen uptake represents basal rather than routine metabolism. This metabolic rate aligns closely with predictions for a marsupial of this body size and dietary specialization, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a diet dominated by leaves and occasional fruits. The measurements were conducted on individuals acclimated to laboratory conditions for several weeks prior to testing, minimizing any confounding effects of capture stress or recent activity. When compared to other phalangerid species, the maximum BMR of Phalanger orientalis suggests a moderate metabolic strategy, neither as low as that of some koala-like specialists nor as high as that of more frugivorous relatives. These data provide a critical baseline for understanding the energetic budget of this species across its life cycle.

Newborn Northern common cuscuses emerge at a remarkably small size, with neonates weighing only 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams] immediately following parturition. This minimal birth mass is characteristic of marsupials, which give birth to highly altricial young that complete much of their development within the maternal pouch. The gestation period underlying this abbreviated in utero development has been documented at 13 days [tg = 13 days] under the species' typical core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a remarkably brief interval that reflects the marsupial reproductive strategy of early parturition followed by extended lactation. Comparative data from the closely related spotted cuscus (Spilocuscus maculatus) informed the birth weight estimate, as direct measurements from Phalanger orientalis neonates remain scarce in the literature. Upon entering the pouch, the neonatal pups immediately attach to a teat and begin an extended period of lactation-dependent growth. This altricial neonate stage is critical for subsequent development, as the newborn mammal must complete organogenesis and significant somatic growth while remaining continuously attached to the maternal teat. The tiny mass of the joey at birth imposes substantial energetic demands on the lactating female, who must provision the developing young with milk rich in proteins and lipids over many months.

Female Northern common cuscuses attain an ultimate adult body mass averaging 2100 grams [Wwi = 2100 grams], though individuals recorded in field surveys span a broader range from approximately 1600 to 5000 grams, reflecting geographic variation and individual condition. This adult body mass places Phalanger orientalis among the larger members of the genus, with females typically exceeding males in size. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, based on extrapolations from the closely related Spilocuscus maculatus under similar thermal conditions, reaches approximately 18.9 years [am = approximately 18.9 years] when maintained at a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable among marsupials of comparable body size and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace, consistent with the species' arboreal, low-metabolism lifestyle. At this age, the oldest documented individuals in captivity approach the maximum, though wild populations likely experience higher mortality rates due to predation and resource limitation. The lifespan places this species within the broader context of slow-living phalangerids, where metabolic rate and reproductive output are traded off against extended survival.

Reproductive output in the Northern common cuscus follows a pattern typical of phalangerid marsupials, with females producing a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] under the species' normal body temperature regime of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Litter size ranges from one to three pups [N_R_i = Litter size ranges from one to three pups], yielding a modest annual reproductive rate that reflects the high per-offspring investment characteristic of arboreal marsupials. The relatively low fecundity is offset by the extensive parental care provided during the prolonged lactation period, which is essential for the development of the altricial young. This combination of a single annual litter with up to three pups per event constrains the species' population growth potential but ensures that each offspring receives sufficient nutritional support for successful maturation. The timing of parturition is closely tied to seasonal resource availability, with births typically coinciding with periods of peak food abundance. The maximum reproductive rate recorded under optimal captive conditions was achieved when females were maintained at their preferred thermal range, highlighting the importance of thermoregulatory stability for successful breeding. These reproductive parameters situate Phalanger orientalis within the broader pattern of slow, K-selected life histories common among tropical arboreal mammals.

The developmental timeline of Phalanger orientalis is characterized by prolonged parental dependency and a delayed onset of reproductive maturity. When maintained at a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], weaning occurs at 270 days since birth [tx = 270 days since birth], marking the transition from exclusive milk feeding to a diet of solid foods. This weaning age is comparatively extended even by marsupial standards, reflecting the slow growth rates associated with the species' folivorous diet and low metabolic expenditure. Following nutritional independence, juveniles continue a prolonged period of somatic growth and behavioral learning before reaching sexual maturity. Puberty is attained at 300 days since birth [tp = 300 days since birth] at this same thermal regime, at which point gonadal maturation commences at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The interval between weaning and puberty represents a critical window during which young cuscuses refine their foraging skills and establish the body condition necessary for future reproductive success. This developmental schedule, with weaning preceding puberty by only approximately one month, suggests a relatively compressed sub-adult phase relative to the total lifespan. The consistency of these developmental milestones under stable thermal conditions indicates that temperature plays a permissive rather than regulatory role in maturation timing, with nutrition likely serving as the primary proximate driver.
